extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (future teachers) writing proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing clear, precise, and readable mathematical proofs for coursework and exposition, aimed at undergraduate students (particularly those training as teachers). Covers prose style, structure, and formula usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in narrative form
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proof should be written as ordinary prose in complete sentences and organized into paragraphs rather than as terse symbolic statements or two-column high-school geometry style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although you may construct a proof with terse symbolic steps, present it as paragraph-style prose when writing up; paragraph-style proofs are easier for human readers to comprehend than symbolic lists or two-column proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proper English
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical writing must follow standard conventions of grammar, usage, punctuation, and spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use complete sentences with correct punctuation (including a period at the end of every sentence), avoid fragments and run-ons, observe subject-verb agreement and parallel structure, and use correct capitalization and spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide preliminary discussion explaining why the theorem might be true, why the proof takes its particular path, and how the result might be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place motivation before the theorem statement, at the beginning of a proof, or at transitions between parts of a proof; include when the proof is complicated or follows an unexpected path so readers get intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of who will read the proof and what background they possess; write to convince a typical member of that audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For homework, write as if convincing a fellow student in the same class; assume the reader knows the same background but not the particular proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the right amount of detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much of the argument to write out based on audience and whether omitted details would be obvious to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an argument seems tedious, work it out fully first; include enough detail to give the reader the 'Aha!' experience and to show graders you worked out the details. Omitting steps is acceptable only if they would be obvious to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clearly what you are proving and label results
rubrics_metrics.description: Each theorem or result should be clearly labeled (Theorem, Proposition, Lemma, Corollary) and stated precisely in one or more English sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not copy the homework statement verbatim; instead state the theorem (e.g., 'Theorem: If x is a real number, then x^2 ≥ 0.'). Use labels to indicate the role of results (proposition = interesting but less important than theorem; lemma = technical step; corollary = immediate consequence). In typeset work use bold/italics or underline in handwritten work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show where proofs begin and end
rubrics_metrics.description: Each proof should begin with the word 'Proof' and end with QED or a closing symbol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with 'Proof' and conclude either with 'QED' or a terminal symbol such as a square to clearly mark the end of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision — define terms and quantify correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: Every term and symbol must have a precise mathematical meaning; expressions must be defined or quantified appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'What does it mean?' for each statement: e.g., if you write f(a) > 0, state whether this is for all a ∈ R, there exists an a ∈ R, or a particular previously-introduced a. Ensure every symbol is defined or quantified before use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with precision — justify every claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Every conclusion must be justified by one of a small set of accepted ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim should be justified by an axiom, a previously proved theorem, a definition, a hypothesis, a previous step in the current proof, or by rules of logic. Justification need not always be written explicitly, but it must be easy for the reader to see how each statement follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write clearly — explain structure and approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the proof comprehensible by describing informally what you will do, carrying out the argument, and then summarizing what was done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For arguments longer than a few sentences, begin with an informal description of the plan (what you'll do and why), state the proof type if nontrivial (e.g., 'We will prove the contrapositive' or 'by contradiction'), intersperse words with formulas, and summarize after completing steps so the reader follows the logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish formal vs. informal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make it easy for the reader to tell which parts are formal (definitions and logical steps) and which are informal (motivation, intuition, sketches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear transitions and phrasing to separate precise formal arguments from intuition or sketch material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person singular sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'we' over 'I' in mathematical exposition when 'we' can reasonably mean 'writer and reader', but use 'I' when referring only to yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'we' for standard exposition ('We will prove the theorem by induction on n'), but if describing a personal anecdote or single-author action, use 'I' (e.g., 'I learned this technique...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid most abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use informal shorthand (e.g., 's.t.', 'w.r.t.', 'w.l.o.g.') in written exposition; only standard formal abbreviations are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abbreviations except those acceptable in formal writing like 'i.e.' and 'e.g.' (use them correctly). The abbreviation 'iff' is discouraged in formal writing and better reserved for notes/blackboard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread
rubrics_metrics.description: Read proofs from beginning to end after finishing to catch errors and sloppy reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful proofreading will reveal many small mistakes; read aloud if helpful to check clarity and grammar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inline vs displayed formulas appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Include single symbols and short formulas inline; display large or important formulas centered on their own line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inline formulas for short expressions (e.g., 'If x is a real number, then x^2 ≥ 0'). Display formulas that are large, important, or will be numbered for later reference. If numbering formulas, be consistent in placement (left or right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Every formula must have a grammatical function
rubrics_metrics.description: No formula (inline or displayed) should stand alone as a sentence; formulas must function grammatically as nouns or clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulas generally serve as (1) noun expressions representing objects or (2) complete symbolic statements acting as clauses. Read sentences aloud to ensure grammatical integration. Example: 'If x > 2, we see that x^2 + x must be greater than 6.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuate displayed formulas correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: If a displayed formula ends a sentence or would require punctuation inline, include the corresponding punctuation after the displayed formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A displayed equation that ends a sentence must be followed by a period. Similarly include commas, semicolons, etc., as required by the surrounding sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation/operator symbols only to connect mathematical symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols like =, >, ∈, ⊆, +, −, ∩ should connect mathematical symbols, not words or English phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'x is a real number that is > 2'; prefer 'x is a real number such that x > 2' or 'x is a real number that is greater than 2.' Examples: (BAD) 'If x is a real number that is > 2...' vs (GOOD) 'If x is a real number such that x > 2, then...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Display built-up expressions and format large fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex expressions (summations, integrals, matrices, large fractions) should be displayed or formatted to fit on a line without disrupting spacing; use slashes for small inline fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write small inline fractions as x/(y+2). If a fraction is large or needs a horizontal bar, display it. Small numerical fractions like 1/2 are acceptable inline if typeset small enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not start a sentence with a mathematical symbol since you cannot capitalize it to mark the start; reword the sentence instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite 'f is a continuous function' as 'The function f is continuous' so the sentence begins with a word, making it easier to recognize sentence boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid placing two formulas separated only by punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not put two formulas next to each other with only a comma or similar punctuation, as they will appear as one long formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpose a word between formulas: instead of 'If x ≠ 0, x^2 > 0' write 'If x ≠ 0, then x^2 > 0.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using logical-symbols in ordinary English sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols for logical terms (∃, ∀, ∧, ∨, ¬, ⇒, ⇔) should not replace English words in normal prose, except in complete symbolic formulas or limited uses of ⇒ and ⇔ connecting formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless writing in symbolic logic, write out 'for all', 'there exists', 'and', 'or', 'not', 'implies'. Acceptable uses: (a) as part of symbolic logic formulas, or (b) using ⇒/⇔ to connect formulas/letters (not full English statements). Examples given: 'We will prove that (a) ⇔ (b) by first showing (a) ⇒ (b) and then (b) ⇒ (a).' (GOOD) vs 'The fact that x is nonzero ⇒ x^2 is positive.' (BAD).
